newsitem.title: UK: Explosive found as N.Ireland marches end.
newsitem.headline: Explosive found as N.Ireland marches end.

text.p: Northern Ireland police on Sunday discovered a large quantity of home-made explosive, a favoured weapon of IRA guerrillas, as the province recovered from a week of violence over Protestant parades.
Police said several hundred pounds (kilos) of explosive had been found in three plastic bins in a coal shed at the back of a house in the Catholic Irish nationalist city of Londonderry.

The find was announced hours after Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, appeared to dash hopes of an immediate IRA ceasefire which would admit his party to slow-moving Northern Ireland peace talks.
Adams said in a statement issued after a week of tension over Protestant Orange Order parades that the surrender of arms held by his guerrilla allies "still remains a major difficulty".
He was responding to Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, who told Sinn Fein on Sunday: "Let the IRA/Sinn Fein make their decision, the ball is in their court."

Adams was echoing the IRA position that "decommissioning" should take place at the end of talks on a settlement between pro-British Unionist and pro-Irish nationalists, not before or even during as Britain has proposed.

It appeared to dash hopes raised by some politicians that the IRA might declare a new ceasefire after the Protestant "marching season", which reached a relatively peaceful climax on Saturday, the order's cherished "Glorious 12th of July".

Adams' statement followed appeals by Britain's new Labour government for an end to the guerrilla Irish Republican Army's (IRA) war against British rule which would earn Sinn Fein a seat at the peace talks within six weeks if it was genuine.
"If people want us to persaude the IRA to end its campaign...then they need to be giving us the ability to do that," Adams said.

He said that although Britain was no longer demanding that the IRA disarm to earn Sinn Fein a seat at the talks, proposals that it surrender weapons during the talks "retain the potential to block progress during negotiations".
The head of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist party, said earlier on Sunday that talk of an IRA truce was "wishful thinking".

Trimble said Britain should abandon hopes of involving Sinn Fein in the talks, which resume on Tuesday after some of the worst rioting the province has seen and a landmark climbdown by the Orange Order over its annual marches.

"What the (British) Prime Minister and the government are trying to do only makes sense on the basis of leaving Sinn fein behind, and consequently for the democratic parties to be discussing among themselves," he said.

He recalled that the IRA injured five members of the security forces in a North Belfast ambush on the eve of the 12th of July when the Orange Order recalls a 1690 Protestant victory over a Catholic king with province-wide marches.
The order scrapped four flashpoint parades under the threat of mass counter demonstrations by Catholics who call them intimidation but went ahead with hundreds of others on Saturday.
Moderate Catholic nationlist leader John Hume hailed the "moral courge"" of the Orange Order for defusing fears of sectarian strife by calling off four controversial marches.
Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) urged all sides to seize a chance for progress.
